summaries.example: Imagine a tiny system that can be in two basic conditions, like a small switch pointing left or right. Quantum mathematics can describe a state made from both possibilities together. When a measuring device checks the system, the theory gives probabilities for the result. The mathematics predicts these results extremely well, even though philosophers and physicists still disagree about what the mathematics says the tiny system is really like.
summaries.summary: Quantum mechanics describes tiny physical systems with mathematics. It uses a special kind of space, called a Hilbert space, to represent the possible states of a system. Vectors in that space stand for states, and operators stand for measurable features such as energy. The theory includes a rule for how a state changes over time and a probability rule for what a measurement may show. These mathematical rules work with great precision. However, people do not agree about what kind of reality lies behind them. The entry focuses mainly on the mathematical structure rather than choosing one interpretation. It also explains that combined systems can have features that are not fixed simply by listing the features of each part. This makes quantum mechanics both powerful and difficult to understand.
key_ideas: Quantum mechanics is a mathematical tool for predicting what happens in the very small world.
Its predictions about measurements are remarkably accurate.
A system’s possible states are represented by vectors in a Hilbert space.
Operators represent measurable features and help describe how states change.
The theory has rules for ordinary time changes and rules for measurement, but how these rules fit together is an important puzzle.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantum mechanics is a foundation for understanding the microscopic world. Its mathematics connects possible states, measurements, probabilities, and changes over time. Learning its basic structure also helps explain why scientists and philosophers ask different questions about what a successful theory is telling us about reality.

important_terms.definition: A complete description of the changing features of a physical system at a particular time.
A mathematical space containing all the possible states of a quantum system.
A mathematical object with length and direction that can represent a possible state.
A mathematical rule that changes one vector into another vector in the same space.
A measurable feature, such as energy, represented in quantum mechanics by a special operator.

questions_to_think_about: Can a mathematical description tell us what the world is really like, or only what we will observe?
Why might a system have several possible measurement results before it is measured?
What should happen when a measuring device meets a system in a mixture of possibilities?

summaries.example: Consider a system with two possible measurement results for an observable, represented by orthogonal state-vectors |A=a1⟩ and |A=a2⟩. A state such as (1/√2)|A=a1⟩ + (1/√2)|A=a2⟩ is a superposition, not itself an eigenstate of that observable. Born’s Rule assigns probability 1/2 to each result. If an apparatus begins in a ready state and interacts with the system, linear Schrödinger evolution produces a superposition correlating each system result with a different apparatus reading. The measurement postulate instead says that one correlated result occurs with the stated probabilities. The tension between these descriptions is the measurement problem.
summaries.summary: The entry presents quantum mechanics first as a mathematical machine and then considers what its mathematics might mean. A system is associated with a Hilbert space: unit vectors represent pure states, while observables are represented by Hermitian operators whose eigenvalues are possible measurement results. Inner products supply geometric notions such as length and orthogonality, and expansion in an orthonormal basis provides coordinates or wave-function representations. Composite systems are represented by tensor products. Importantly, not every composite state factors into one state for each component, so the state of a whole may contain structure not fixed by the states of its parts. Dynamics has two forms in the standard presentation. Schrödinger evolution is deterministic, linear, and unitary. Measurement is described by collapse to an eigenstate, with outcome probabilities given by Born’s Rule. The entry emphasizes that it remains unsettled, in the theory’s own terms, which situations count as measurements and whether collapse is fundamental. Applying both rules to a measuring apparatus creates the measurement problem. Interpretations attempt to explain what the formalism says about the world, but the entry itself concentrates on the mathematical core.
key_ideas: Quantum mechanics is mathematically precise as a predictive theory, while its interpretation—the account of what the formalism says exists—is disputed.
Pure states are represented by unit vectors in Hilbert space; more generally, states are represented by density operators, including mixed states.
Hermitian operators represent observables, and their eigenvalues are possible measurement results.
Schrödinger evolution is deterministic, linear, and unitary, whereas the measurement postulate introduces probabilistic collapse.
The tensor-product structure of composite systems allows facts about a whole system that are not determined by independently specifying facts about its parts.
The measurement problem arises from the apparent conflict between universal linear evolution and collapse during measurement.
summaries.why_it_matters: Quantum mechanics shows how a theory can make extraordinarily accurate predictions while leaving major questions about reality open. Its Hilbert-space structure explains why quantum states differ from classical states, why composite systems have surprising relations to their parts, and why measurement is philosophically difficult. Understanding the formalism is therefore essential before evaluating competing interpretations.

important_terms.definition: A mathematical structure consisting of vectors, an inner product, and a completeness condition; in quantum mechanics it represents a system’s state-space.
A mathematical object with magnitude and direction; state-vectors represent pure states.
A rule on a vector space that maps vectors to vectors; linear operators preserve addition and multiplication by scalars.
An operator with an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors and real eigenvalues; it represents a physical quantity in the theory.
A vector that an operator changes only by multiplying it by a number; that number is its eigenvalue.
A rule assigning probabilities to measurement outcomes using the squared magnitude of an inner product.
The rule that an ideal measurement leaves a system in an eigenstate associated with the observed result.
The mathematical construction used for the state-space of a composite system; it permits states not expressible as products of component states.

questions_to_think_about: If every physical interaction follows linear Schrödinger evolution, what makes some interactions measurements?
Does a superposition describe a physical condition, incomplete knowledge, or something else?
Why does the tensor product challenge the idea that a whole is fully determined by its separately described parts?
Can a theory be empirically successful while leaving its underlying ontology unsettled?

summaries.example: Suppose a game device has two possible readouts, red and blue. Before checking it, its quantum state might be represented by a combination of a red-state vector and a blue-state vector. The mathematics does not simply say that the device is secretly red or secretly blue. Instead, Born’s Rule gives probabilities for the readout. Now connect the device to a display. Ordinary time evolution links the red possibility to one display state and the blue possibility to another. The mathematical result is a combined state containing both links, while the measurement rule says that an actual reading has one result. Explaining how these descriptions fit together is the measurement problem.
summaries.summary: Quantum mechanics is presented as a highly successful mathematical framework for predicting the behavior of microscopic systems or, at minimum, the effects those systems have on measuring instruments. The entry separates this predictive and mathematical success from the unsettled question of interpretation: what sort of world, if any, does the formalism describe beneath the observations? Each system has a state-space, and in quantum mechanics the relevant state-spaces are Hilbert spaces. These contain vectors, which can be added and multiplied by numbers, and an inner product, which supplies ideas such as length and perpendicularity. A chosen orthonormal basis lets us express any vector through coefficients; in infinite-dimensional settings, related coefficient functions are called wave functions. Operators map vectors to vectors, and Hermitian operators represent observables. Their eigenvalues are the possible results of measurements. The tensor product builds the state-space of a combined system. It allows composite states that are not simple products of component states, raising questions about whether the properties of a whole are fixed by the properties of its parts. Finally, Schrödinger’s equation gives deterministic, linear, unitary evolution, while the collapse postulate and Born’s Rule describe probabilistic measurement outcomes. The unresolved tension between these rules is the measurement problem.
key_ideas: Quantum mechanics predicts microscopic measurement results with exceptional accuracy, but its picture of underlying reality is disputed.
A physical quantity is called an observable in quantum-mechanical language and is represented mathematically by an operator.
Vectors can be combined into superpositions, and a superposition can lead to several possible measurement results with calculated probabilities.
A composite system has a tensor-product state-space, and some states of the whole cannot be represented as a simple product of states for its parts.
The theory describes continuous, deterministic evolution with Schrödinger’s equation and probabilistic change during measurement.
The measurement problem concerns the unresolved relationship between these two kinds of evolution.
summaries.why_it_matters: The entry provides the mathematical background needed to discuss the philosophy of quantum mechanics responsibly. It shows that many puzzling features—superposition, incompatible observables, composite-system structure, and measurement difficulties—arise from the relations among vectors and operators, not merely from a failure of ordinary language. It also distinguishes secure predictive machinery from open questions about what the machinery means.

important_terms.definition: The complete condition of a physical system, including the properties that can change with time.
The set of mathematically possible states for a system; in quantum mechanics it has the structure of a Hilbert space.
A vector space with an inner product and a completeness property; quantum states are represented within it.
A mathematical object that can be added to other vectors or multiplied by numbers; it represents a possible pure state.
A rule that maps vectors in a space to other vectors; operators represent physical quantities or changes.
A special operator whose possible measurement values are its eigenvalues.
The probability rule connecting a state-vector with a possible measurement outcome.
The construction that combines the state-spaces of two systems into the state-space of the pair.

questions_to_think_about: What is gained by representing states as points or vectors in a mathematical space?
Why does a superposition differ from an ordinary list of our uncertainty about a state?
If a composite system has a state not built from separate component states, what does that suggest about wholes and parts?
Should measurement be treated as a special physical process, or should the ordinary evolution rule apply everywhere?
